content: Hello Arklib contributors! I'm working on making an up-to-date bibliography for ArkLib and conventions for referencing papers in the codebase, see draft PR here. Are there any standard references or important papers that are not yet included in references.bib, or elsewhere in the repository, but should be? Also hoping for feedback on the referencing style proposed here. Thanks in advance!

Hey team!

Great work on centralizing the references.bib file, Derek — that’s a solid improvement for maintainability.

My feedback and question focus on the citation style used in the source Lean files, which Derek made changes in commit 12c732b. While the simplified format is cleaner, I think it abstracts away context that’s especially valuable for a high-assurance library like ArkLib.
Comparison:

  • Current (simplified): [Lin, S., Chung, W., and Han, Y.S., *Novel polynomial basis and its application to reed-solomon erasure codes*][LCH14]

  • Preferred (academic/cryptobib style): [LCH14] Sian-Jheng Lin, Wei-Ho Chung, and Yunghsiang S. Han. “Novel Polynomial Basis and Its Application to Reed–Solomon Erasure Codes”. In: IEEE 55th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science. 2014, pp. 316–325. doi: 10.1109/FOCS.2014.41.

I believe adopting the more verbose, academic format—which is the standard in cryptography and formal verification — adds significant value because:

  1. Provenance: It instantly distinguishes peer-reviewed, top-tier conference-level results (FOCS, CRYPTO, etc.) from unverified preprints or technical reports.
  2. Context: Venue and year let readers judge "freshness" and scholarly authority at first glance without having to context-switch to the .bib file back-and-forth.
  3. Permanence: DOIs are persistent identifiers; article titles and URLs can rot or change.
  4. Completeness & Authority: As Quang Dao pointed out when I discussed this with him, the goal should be to include all bibliographic details, effectively matching the standard set by cryptobib. This means:

    * Listing all authors explicitly (avoiding "et al." truncation where possible).
    * Using full names rather than just initials.
    * Providing the complete reference in a structured, readable format directly in the docstring.
    * A typical citation in crypto.bib looks like below, we might use it as source for references.bib too if possible.

@InProceedings{FOCS:BCIKS20,
  author =       "Eli {Ben-Sasson} and
                  Dan Carmon and
                  Yuval Ishai and
                  Swastik Kopparty and
                  Shubhangi Saraf",
  title =        "Proximity Gaps for Reed-Solomon Codes",
  pages =        "900--909",
  editor =       focs20ed,
  booktitle =    focs20name,
  address =      focs20addr,
  month =        focs20month,
  publisher =    focspub,
  year =         2020,
  doi =          "10.1109/FOCS46700.2020.00088",
}
  1. Auditability: For a library focused on verification, having self-contained, authoritative citations in the source is a direct aid to auditability and trust. The extra few lines provide permanent, searchable context.

My suggestion is a hybrid approach that gives us the best of both worlds:

  • Keep the centralized references.bib for tooling and consistency.
  • Adopt the full academic citation style (akin to cryptobib's output) in our Lean docstrings and documentation.

This keeps our source code authoritative, self-documenting, and ready for rigorous audit, which aligns perfectly with ArkLib's high-assurance goals.

What are your thoughts on this?

Hey @Chung Thai Nguyen thank you for this, this is great feedback. My goal with the references PR (now merged) was to adopt the conventions of Mathlib and CSLib, since there is in principle a goal to upstream some of the Arklib stuff into each of these libraries. I don't know about the rest of the community, but my hesitation for including the full academic/cryptobib style in the docstings is that it (1) doesn't conform to Mathlib and CSlib conventions, and (2) is a little bit cumbersome to write. I appreciate that it disambiguates between different versions of papers and includes e.g. the DOI, but my preference would be to include all of the data you mention in the citation in references.bib and then to disambiguate between e.g. preprints or different versions of papers by having multiple entries in references.bib and using the correct identifier, e.g. [LCH14]. Does that make sense? Any thoughts on this?

That’s a very good point about following Mathlib/CSLib conventions and avoiding the overhead of verbose in-file citations.

My thoughts are as follows:

  1. For generic infrastructure/support files (CodingTheory/Basic.lean, UniPoly/Basic.lean, some Prelude.lean, etc.): we usually don’t need many citations. These files are meant to be broadly reusable foundations rather than literature-specific developments, so this aligns well with Mathlib/CSLib style.

  2. For key files containing paper-specific results (BCIKS20, STIR, WHIR, etc.): I’d still recommend full bibliographic citations in the docstring at the top of the files, following conventions in the crypto papers we are formalizing. These main files are essentially mini-papers, full in-file citations provide immediate context (authors, venue, DOI) without jumping to a .bib, making them self-contained and audit-ready. This is also a good way to demonstrate the reliability and provenance of the formalization, in addition to giving clear attribution to the original authors (also it looks more professional).

    In practice, for these key files, having ~12 lines of citations for 3 references is negligible compared to the thousands (or tens of thousands) of lines of code in their specific folder; e.g. for FRI, citations can be centralized in General.lean.

This keeps us aligned with upstream conventions while strengthening the credibility and auditability of the formalization where it matters most. What do you think? I’d like to hear people’s views on this so we can make a well-considered decision. The changes are already in place, so there’s no urgency to iterate again immediately — the goal here is to gather feedback and converge on a unified, well-reasoned approach in the long run.

  • Plus that I suggest us to build a page for references in the documentation site like this https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/references.html

That's a good point, I thought the current docgen would be doing this but indeed it isn't.

leaving a short summary of wat we discussed wrt to this during the call today:

  • Default option is to leave the standard as it is now; at least we now have a standard.
  • With regards to verbose docstrings and referencing in the style of an academic citation: one point to consider is that in many cases we may be formalizing a paper as it is on eprint/arxiv because it was updated after the conference/journal publication, and the conference/journal version may also be an abridged version. IT seems to me that we should reference the file we are actually looking at. In addition to this (not mentioned during the call, adding this now) I would strongly urge us to only refer to open access papers given people looking at ArkLib may not have an academic affiliation that gives them access to all conference papers (of course many are open access, but nonetheless).
  • Let's keep the conversation open.
